extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, PR teams, and content/marketing practitioners who write and distribute press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting news-focused press releases (product launches, company news, events, data reports) that attract journalist attention and secure coverage. Covers essential elements, type-specific sections, templates, length, assets, and distribution tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release purpose: informative and news-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases are structured, news–focused statements designed to inform media and secure coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on being an informational source for journalists rather than editorial or inspirational content. Tailor releases to journalists’ needs by prioritizing concise, relevant, and well-proofed content over promotional fluff. Aim to be newsworthy to avoid becoming ‘a waste of time and money.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline is one of the most essential parts of your press release — concise, engaging, and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on why the release is essential to the audience, not why your company is excellent. Use a strong title that states why the news matters to readers and makes them want to read more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline presents the date you publish the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the dateline simple — it’s a critical element but don’t overcomplicate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-in (intro / lead paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead-in is the beginning of the first sentence and should summarize the most critical aspects of the announcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For branding consistency, the lead-in should always be the same across your releases (often written ahead of time as part of a press kit). The lead paragraph should capture the core news succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key facts / key findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Add key facts so journalists can quickly scan and extract the most crucial information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only newsworthy takeaways — if a finding merely reiterates a well-known fact, leave it out. For data/reports, try to include 8–13 key findings. Use bullets for readability and to help journalists identify takeaways quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always include at least one quote in all press releases; ideal quotes are two to four sentences long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes can come from executives, project leads, partners, customers, or other stakeholders. You can include multiple quotes when relevant (e.g., from a new partner, hire, or customer). Customer quotes serve as third-party validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-to-action (CTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: All press releases should have a call to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CTAs can be event registration links, landing pages, or a link to the company homepage. For report releases, the CTA will often drive downloads or sign-ups for the full report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard paragraph at the end that provides background information about the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The boilerplate should outline what the company does and can usually be pulled from your press kit. Keep it brief and factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact information & PR gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact information for the press and designate PR as the gatekeeper for inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use someone on the PR team (internal or agency) as the primary contact so executives aren’t inundated. Provide clear contact details to facilitate follow-up from journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional media / assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide unique media assets (data, infographics, videos, product images, headshots) to increase reach and make journalists’ jobs easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include assets whenever possible — they make releases stand out and give journalists elements to visualize. Examples: product image, executive headshot, infographic, or video.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product launch specifics (product specs & availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: For product launches, include key differentiators of the product and availability details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call out features that make the product stand out from competitors or previous versions. Reference product specs or marketing materials and state launch date, availability, and where to purchase or learn more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company news specifics (significance & highlights)
rubrics_metrics.description: When announcing company news (hires, mergers, awards, milestones), include at least one specific highlight that makes the news significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the news impacts those outside the organization (e.g., new VP’s background and what they’ll bring, the main contributor to an award). Tie the announcement back to its relevance for the wider audience or industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event announcement specifics (the 5 W’s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Event press releases must include the 5 W’s: who, what, when, where, and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also include who should attend and registration details (where/how to register). Scan event coverage in target publications to ensure you include common elements and themes they expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-driven report specifics (key takeaways & demographics)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reports and surveys, highlight the most insightful takeaways and provide survey demographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer brief analysis to intrigue journalists but not give everything away; include demographics so journalists can judge fit for their audience. These releases may be longer (often >1,000 words) and should include a CTA to download the full report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended word counts and concision guidance for different release types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for around 600–800 words for news, events, and product launches. Data-driven reports can go well over 1,000 words because they include critical takeaways and analysis. Keep language concise and focused on newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully proofread press releases to avoid errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small mistakes reduce credibility. Re-read multiple times and consider tools like Grammarly. Ensure claims are verified and avoid unverified assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a strategic plan to distribute the press release so it reaches the right audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use digital PR tools (e.g., BuzzStream) and targeted email outreach. For email pitching, use templates, set sequences and follow-ups, track opens/clicks, and personalize outreach to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: What not to include (avoidances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid irrelevant information, jargon, unverified claims, and personal opinions that don’t support the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on newsworthy content that interests the media and your audience. If an enhancement only matters to existing customers, prefer email campaigns over a public press release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure / core components
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical press release structure: headline, dateline, introduction (lead), body, quote, boilerplate, CTA, and contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three core components to always get right are the headline, the lead paragraph, and the body. Use the canonical order to meet journalist expectations and make scanning easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting for readability (bullets & layout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bullets and clear formatting to break down complexity and make content easier to scan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bullets can call out product features, key findings, or highlights. Examples on the page show bullets improving readability and helping journalists extract facts quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third‑party validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include third‑party or customer quotes to provide external validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customer quotes or partner statements act as social proof and can strengthen the story’s credibility and newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional end notation (-30-, ###, -END-)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a notation at the end of the press release to indicate the end of the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common traditional notations are “30”, “###”, or “-END-”, a holdover from press telegraphy days in the U.S. Some outlets still expect or recognize this convention.
